name: rmz (FUC, Rust multi-threaded rm)
baseline: GNU rm -r (coreutils, C); the same table also lists find -delete and rsync --delete
workload: Deleting directory trees generated by ftzz (10 to 1M files, 0 B or 1 GiB total, default depth, depth 0, and 5 files per directory), timed with hyperfine --warmup 3 -N on an xfs /tmp.
claimed_speedup: 1M files, 0 B: rmz 4.711 s +- 0.649 vs rm -r 9.491 s +- 0.059 (table Relative column: rm -r 2.01 +- 0.28 times slower). 1M files, 1 GiB: rmz 6.559 s vs rm -r 23.354 s (3.56 +- 0.29). 100,000 files, 0 B: rmz 459.3 ms vs rm -r 873.7 ms (1.90 +- 0.41). 100,000 files in one flat directory (depth 0): rmz 830.7 ms vs rm -r 847.1 ms (1.02, parity).
compiler_and_flags: cargo b --workspace --release; Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true, panic = abort. rustc version not stated. GNU rm is the distro binary (version not stated).
hardware: Intel i7-7700, 15 GiB RAM, Linux 5.14.0-162.18.1.el9_1.x86_64, /tmp on xfs (/dev/sda6)
stars_or_usage: 535 stars; packaged in several distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Linux is the primary target (macOS and Windows fall back to the rayon-style implementation). Fewer options than coreutils rm. Uses far more total CPU time (System 18.65 s vs 8.77 s at 1M files, 0 B) because it deletes with many threads, so on a busy machine the wall-clock gain shrinks.
caveats: The win is parallel tree deletion, not Rust code generation: the single-threaded Rust rm_stdlib baseline in the same table matches GNU rm (9.345 s vs 9.491 s at 1M files). A flat directory shows no gain (1.02). One machine, one filesystem (xfs on a SATA partition), a warm cache is not mentioned either way. GNU coreutils version and rustc version are not stated. The author's technical overview (alexsaveau.dev/blog/fuc, linked from the README) could not be opened from this environment.
found_via: Blogs / talks: the README of SUPERCILEX/fuc links the author's blog post 'fuc' and a comparisons folder; found by checking READMEs of Rust replacements for GNU coreutils (the WebSearch queries on Rust-vs-C rewrites gave only generic hits)
why_faster: The opened pages state none beyond 'performance focused'; the comparison variants show the gain comes from multithreaded traversal and deletion (rm_stdlib single-threaded 9.345 s, rm_rayon 5.689 s, rmz 4.711 s at 1M files, 0 B) plus tuning over a plain rayon version. Mechanism is inferred from the table (derived from page data), not quoted from the author.

name: cpz (FUC, Rust multi-threaded cp)
baseline: GNU cp -r (coreutils, C); the same table also lists rsync, tar piping, fcp, xcp and wcp
workload: Copying directory trees generated by ftzz (10 to 1M files, 0 B or 1 GiB total, default depth, depth 0, 5 files per directory) with hyperfine --warmup 3 -N on an xfs /tmp.
compiler_and_flags: cargo b --workspace --release; Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true, panic = abort. rustc version not stated. GNU cp is the distro binary (version not stated).
hardware: Intel i7-7700, 15 GiB RAM, Linux 5.14.0-162.18.1.el9_1.x86_64, /tmp on xfs (/dev/sda6)
stars_or_usage: 535 stars; packaged in several distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Linux is the primary target (other platforms use the rayon-style implementation). Non-goal: compatibility with coreutils cp options. Much higher total CPU time than cp (System 23.7 s vs 15.3 s at 1M files, 0 B).
caveats: The win is parallel copying, not Rust code generation: the single-threaded Rust cp_stdlib in the same table matches GNU cp (19.496 s vs 18.436 s at 1M files, 0 B). Copies are source and destination on the same xfs filesystem on one machine; the variance on the cpz rows is large (+- 0.976 s at 1M files). GNU coreutils and rustc versions are not stated. The author's blog overview could not be opened from this environment.
found_via: Blogs / talks: README of SUPERCILEX/fuc (links the author's blog and a comparisons folder), found while checking Rust replacements of GNU coreutils
why_faster: The opened pages state none beyond 'performance focused'; the table indicates multithreaded directory copying (cp_stdlib single-threaded 19.496 s, cp_rayon 5.854 s, cpz 5.076 s at 1M files, 0 B). Inferred from the table (derived from page data), not quoted from the author.

name: fast_rsync (Dropbox, Rust SIMD rsync algorithm)
baseline: librsync (C), through the librsync Rust bindings: whole::signature, whole::delta, whole::patch
workload: rsync signature calculation, delta computation (64 KB edit, random data, pathological collision case) and delta application on 4 MiB buffers (16 KiB for the pathological librsync run), criterion benchmarks in benches/rsync_bench.rs.
claimed_speedup: Signature of 4 MiB: fast_rsync 1.0696 ms (3.6519 GiB/s) vs librsync 5.8521 ms (683.51 MiB/s), README says 6X on AVX2 and 3-4X on SSE2-only CPUs. Delta, 64 KB edit: 7.0596 ms vs 7.4649 ms. Delta, random: 38.317 ms vs 42.758 ms. Pathological 16384-byte case: 6.2550 ms vs 50.185 ms (about 8x, derived from page data); the 4 MiB pathological run is too slow for librsync and is not listed. Apply: 284.20 us vs 400.30 us.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6820HQ @ 2.70 GHz (AVX2), described by the authors as a noisy laptop
tradeoffs: Only the legacy MD4 signature format is supported, not BLAKE2, and MD4 is insecure, so every applied delta must be verified with another hash. SIMD on x86, x86-64 and aarch64 with runtime detection. In-memory buffers only.
caveats: Only the signature step (SIMD rolling checksum and MD4) is a large win; the two realistic delta rows are 6% and 12% faster and the apply row 1.4x. The 8x pathological row reflects collision detection that librsync lacks (different behaviour, not only speed). Compiler flags, build profile of the librsync C library and librsync version are not stated in the README; benches/rsync_bench.rs was not opened, so the harness is unchecked (a verifier may lift the tier if the flags are visible there). Single noisy laptop. Not updated since 2024.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Rust ports of C libraries that beat the original; README benchmark section of dropbox/fast_rsync
why_faster: README: SIMD operations (AVX2 gives the 6X on signatures) for the rolling checksum and MD4; delta rows are bound by single-block MD4 and by hash-map lookups where Rust's built-in HashMap gives 'a slight advantage'; pathological inputs are detected instead of degrading.

name: procs (c-blake, Nim ps, pgrep and pkill replacement: pd, pf, pk)
baseline: procps ps ('/bin/ps ax'), pgrep and pkill (C)
workload: Listing all processes with a minimal format (pid and command) to /dev/null, and finding a process by name over roughly 200 to 320 processes (pf -e1 vs pgrep -x), measured with the author's tim/tails tools under chrt 99 taskset.
claimed_speedup: README footnote: pd -f%p %c 2.8576 ms +- 0.0070 vs /bin/ps ax 5.0281 ms +- 0.0063 (README says roughly 2X; about 1.76x derived from page data); with process typology and highlights on, 3.9739 ms +- 0.0044, 1.27X faster than stock ps; pgrep and pkill are 5.025 +- 0.015X and 5.745 +- 0.016X slower than pf and pk on a 4-core and a 20-core CPU. bench.sh comments: pf -e1 init 1014.1 us vs pgrep -x init 7724 us (i7-6700K, 'up to 7.617 times faster') and 582.7 us vs 5539.6 us (i7-1370P, 9.507 times).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README build line is 'nim c -d:release --path:../cligen procs' (C backend compiler version not stated); procps version not stated
hardware: i7-6700K (no HT, 4.7 GHz) and i7-1370P in bench.sh; the machine for the README ps timings is not named
tradeoffs: Linux /proc only. Fewer canned formats than ps (it is a construction toolkit with config files); pd/pf/pk are symlinks to one binary. Author calls it 'a work in progress'.
caveats: The gains come from doing less work (reading only /proc/PID/stat when the format needs nothing else, where procps opens and parses both stat and status), so it is a different, narrower program rather than the same algorithm. Author says there are configurations where ps can be faster. The README timing machine and flags are unstated; bench.sh needs the author's tim and tails tools. Millisecond-scale wins on a single-user tool.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Nim/D/Zig tools with README timings against C utilities (c-blake GitHub projects), after the Nim topic pages gave nothing
why_faster: README: 'tries hard not to make unnecessary system calls', for example only opening /proc/PID/stat for a pid-and-command format while procps ps also opens and parses /proc/PID/status (the author says this makes pd roughly 2X faster).

name: mk1 (c-blake/bu, Nim up-to-date check for 1-to-1 build rules)
baseline: ninja (C++) and GNU make (C); the table also times a bash while-read loop
workload: Up-to-dateness check of 40,000 input/output file pairs in /dev/shm (nothing to rebuild), timed with the author's ru tool; mk1 reads a precomputed list of path pairs and prints the commands to run.
claimed_speedup: mk1 0.039390 s wall vs ninja with .ninja_log present ('no work to do') 0.119358 s (about 3.0x, README says ~3X faster than ninja's best case), ninja without a log 7.777944 s, ninja with the author's restat hack 0.410272 s, GNU make 1.550844 s (README: about 40X worse than mk1), bash loop 0.151993 s (about 4X).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for mk1 (Nim build flags); the page says the machine runs 'Linux 6.2.10 built w/gcc-12', wording unclear whether this refers to the kernel or the binaries; ninja and make versions not stated
hardware: Intel i7-1270P (Alder Lake), Linux 6.2.10, RAM file system (/dev/shm)
tradeoffs: Only handles the case where each output comes from exactly one input by one rule; no dependency graph, no depfile handling, no rule language, and it emits commands for a shell to run rather than running them.
caveats: Compares a deliberately restricted tool with general build systems on a special case; ninja's cost is dominated by its log handling and the author's own hacks. Different problem from ninja's, so same_algorithm is false. Build flags for mk1 and tool versions are missing; the shell script on the page is complete and short, so a verifier could rerun it. First-party measurement by the author, single machine.
found_via: Blogs / talks: c-blake/bu doc pages with README-level timings against C tools
why_faster: Page: only a freshness check for many 1-to-1 pairs is done (about 60 lines of Nim originally, about 150 now, per the page's footnote), with no graph or log; the author attributes make's cost to subshell delegation and ninja's best case to its .ninja_log reuse.

name: dups (c-blake/bu, Nim duplicate-file finder)
workload: Finding sets of files with identical contents in a fully RAM-cached test case (size, hash and compare strategies).
claimed_speedup: 'I continue to benchmark it as ~2X faster than jdupes in a fully RAM-cached test case'; the page adds that uncached runs are dominated by I/O speed and organization.
tradeoffs: Default hash is wyhash, so equal hashes can be false positives unless --cmp is given (sorting or compare can be slow with many large same-size files); options differ from jdupes.
caveats: One sentence of prose with no script, file counts, machine, jdupes version or flags; the cached-only condition removes the I/O bound that dominates real use. Different default (a non-cryptographic hash) than jdupes, which weakens the comparison. A rr/du/find speed claim for the same author is recorded separately under cligen.
found_via: Blogs / talks: c-blake/bu doc pages; 'Motivation' section of doc/dups.md

name: cligen/dents (c-blake, Nim fast directory walker behind find, ls and du)
baseline: GNU find, GNU ls -1AUR and GNU du (C); BSD find and fd are also named for find
workload: Recursive tree walk of /usr printing paths (find), listing with ls -1AUR and ls -s1AUR --color=none to /dev/null, and du totalling st_blocks.
claimed_speedup: Doc comments in dents.nim: find '2.75-4.5X faster than GNU find /usr; 1.7x faster than BSD find|fd'; ls1AU '-r0 is 1.7-2.25x faster than GNU ls -1AUR --color=none /usr >/dev/null'; lss1AU '1.45-2.0x faster than ls -s1AUR'; bu/doc/du.md: 'my 1.4-2x faster file tree walk' for a mostly compatible GNU du replacement.
stars_or_usage: 584 stars (cligen); used by the c-blake/bu tools
tradeoffs: Linux-oriented (raw getdents64, optional custom kernel batch-syscall module that is not mainline). Not a general find: no expression language; the du clone drops several options and uses PCRE patterns.
caveats: The numbers are one-line source comments with no machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions or script; ranges are given without the raw timings. GNU find worries about arbitrary depth, which the author says he has never seen exceed 30, so the walker trades generality for speed. The 'faster than fd' phrasing in the comment is ambiguous.
found_via: Blogs / talks: c-blake/bu doc/du.md and doc/newest.md claims traced to cligen/dents.nim
why_faster: dents.nim header: raw getdents64 saves one fstat per directory compared with opendir or fdopendir, openat/fstatat remove most full-path handling, and an optimistic open after d_type avoids lstat; the author also notes GNU find's handling of arbitrary filesystem depth.

name: Stylo (servo/stylo, Rust parallel CSS style engine of Firefox Quantum)
baseline: Gecko's previous serial C++ style system (Firefox 56 and earlier); not a library that can be rebuilt at -O3
workload: CSS style resolution in Firefox, parallelised over the DOM tree with work stealing, versus the old C++ style system.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (pages not opened): Mozilla Hacks 'Inside a super fast CSS engine: Quantum CSS (aka Stylo)' says the parallel engine can run up to 2 or 4 or even 18 times faster; the Rust blog 'Fearless Concurrency in Firefox Quantum' reports a 30% page-load speedup for Amazon's homepage.
stars_or_usage: 340 stars (Servo's downstream copy); ships in Firefox since version 57
tradeoffs: Tied to the Servo/Gecko style data structures; the repo is a downstream sync of mozilla-central. Parallel gain needs multiple cores and large DOMs.
caveats: Numbers are from search-result snippets of Mozilla and Rust blog posts (blog.rust-lang.org did not resolve from this environment and hacks.mozilla.org was not fetched under the same egress policy), so no number was verified against its page. The range 2x to 18x is a best-case spread without workload or hardware; the 30% figure is page load, not style time. Part of the speedup came from redesign and optimisations borrowed from other engines, so the parallelism gain cannot be isolated, and the baseline is a non-reproducible internal C++ system. The repo README has no benchmarks.
found_via: WebSearch 'Quantum CSS Stylo parallel style system faster than Gecko C++ benchmark speedup Rust'; github.com/servo/stylo opened for license, stars and commit date
why_faster: Per the search snippets: Rust's ownership rules let the team parallelise style computation safely with the rayon work-stealing library after two earlier C++ attempts failed; part of the gain is attributed to the redesign.
